title: NIH and CDC Budgets Gutted: $18 Billion Cut, 694 Grants Canceled
description_short: NIH and CDC Budgets Gutted: $18 Billion Cut, 694 Grants Canceled
description_medium: The Trump administration’s fiscal 2026 budget request proposed reducing NIH funding by $18 billion and nearly halving the CDC budget. Separately, NIH terminated 694 research grants worth $1.81 billion between February 28 and April 8, 2025. Researchers also reported lower NIH award totals early in the year than in the same period of 2024. The proposed budget cuts and completed grant cancellations were distinct actions.
description_long: The Trump administration’s fiscal 2026 budget request proposed cutting National Institutes of Health funding by $18 billion, about 40 percent, and reducing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention budget by nearly half. Separately, NIH terminated 694 research grants worth $1.81 billion between February 28 and April 8, 2025. Those cancellations included $506 million in grants from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases and $224 million from the National Institute on Minority Health and Health Disparities. A New York Times analysis found NIH awards were $1.6 billion lower in the first months of 2025 than during the same period in 2024, a 20 percent decline. The CDC proposal included cuts to chronic disease prevention, gun-violence injury research, and other programs. The budget request had not itself become law, while the grant terminations had already occurred. The two developments therefore describe separate reductions: research awards ended during the fiscal year and a proposed budget for the next fiscal year. Researchers and public-health groups raised concerns about interrupted studies and diminished prevention capacity. The reported grant totals document financial decisions, but do not by themselves quantify resulting effects on patients or public health.

title: Trump's 77% trade-deficit reduction claim relies on selective monthly comparison
description_short: Trump's 77% trade-deficit reduction claim relies on selective monthly comparison
description_medium: Trump said in January 2026 that the U.S. trade deficit had fallen by 77%. FactCheck.org found the figure reflected a comparison between January and October 2025 monthly deficits rather than the full-year trend. After full-year data were released, FactCheck.org reported that the 2025 goods-and-services trade deficit was only 0.2% lower than in 2024. The entry should be dated to the 2026 claim/fact-check period.
description_long: In January 2026, Donald Trump said the U.S. trade deficit had fallen by 77 percent. FactCheck.org traced the figure to a comparison between the monthly deficit in January 2025 and the monthly deficit in October, rather than a comparison of annual totals. The two selected months showed a sharp decline, but they did not establish the trend across the year. After full-year data became available, FactCheck.org reported that the 2025 goods-and-services trade deficit was 0.2 percent lower than in 2024. That result was a near-flat annual change, not the 77 percent reduction claimed from the monthly comparison. The fact-check illustrates why time periods matter when evaluating a headline economic statistic: a change between two individual months can differ substantially from the change between full calendar years. It also separates the president’s public figure from the later calculation using full-year data. The comparison addressed the aggregate trade deficit and did not, by itself, measure the effect of any single tariff or identify the cause of the small annual change. The eventual annual figures supplied a more complete basis for evaluating the claim than the two-month comparison available when Trump made it.

title: UAE and Qatar Invest Hundreds of Millions in Kushner's Affinity Partners
description_short: UAE and Qatar Invest Hundreds of Millions in Kushner's Affinity Partners
description_medium: Wealth funds in the UAE and Qatar invested hundreds of millions of dollars with Jared Kushner's private equity firm Affinity Partners, the New York Times reported in March 2023. The Emiratis invested more than $200 million through a sovereign wealth fund, while a Qatari entity put in a similar sum. Kushner formed the Miami-based Affinity Partners in 2021 after leaving the White House.
description_long: Jared Kushner formed Affinity Partners in 2021 after leaving his role as a senior adviser in the Trump White House. The Miami-based private-equity firm later received substantial commitments from Gulf investors. In March 2023, The New York Times reported that an Emirati sovereign wealth fund had invested more than $200 million and that a Qatari entity had committed a similar sum. These were separate investments in Kushner’s private firm, not government payments to him personally. The financing drew attention because Kushner had recently served in government and had worked on Middle East policy, including efforts connected to the Abraham Accords. The overlap prompted questions about the potential for perceived conflicts when former officials pursue private business with foreign state-linked investors. The reported commitments document the investors and approximate amounts, but do not establish that a diplomatic decision was exchanged for investment or that the governments directed the funds for an improper purpose. Kushner’s business received money after his government service, and the public concern centered on transparency, access, and the appearance of influence. The account does not describe a finding of wrongdoing by Affinity Partners or its investors.

title: January 2025 Immigration Executive Orders Do Not Suspend Habeas Corpus
description_short: January 2025 Immigration Executive Orders Do Not Suspend Habeas Corpus
description_medium: Trump's January 20, 2025 executive orders on immigration - including 'Protecting the American People Against Invasion' - direct enforcement of immigration laws and detention capabilities but do not suspend habeas corpus. The Alien Enemies Act was invoked later, in March 2025, in the Tren de Aragua deportation episode, and habeas corpus review remained available in federal courts. The card's claim of a day-one habeas suspension is unsupported.
description_long: On January 20, 2025, Donald Trump signed the executive order “Protecting the American People Against Invasion.” It directed federal agencies to pursue immigration enforcement, detention, and removal measures and instructed officials to use available authority to carry out those policies. The order did not suspend habeas corpus or state that immigrants could be held indefinitely without judicial review. The Alien Enemies Act entered a separate dispute in March 2025, when the administration relied on it to deport Venezuelan men it accused of belonging to Tren de Aragua. That later action generated litigation over whether people facing removal could challenge their detention and deportation in court. Keeping the events separate matters: the January order established enforcement priorities, while the later invocation of the 1798 statute involved a distinct legal authority and specific removals. Habeas corpus review remained available in federal courts. The record therefore supports describing a broad enforcement directive and the subsequent legal conflict, but not a presidential order that eliminated the constitutional remedy. The claimed day-one habeas suspension did not occur.

title: Trump signs childhood-vaccine executive order and invokes autism in remarks
description_short: Trump signs childhood-vaccine executive order and invokes autism in remarks
description_medium: On August 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420 revising federal childhood-vaccine recommendations, including recommending separate administration of MMR components once available and spacing immunizations across visits. In remarks at the signing, Trump said the initiative involved autism and reiterated claims linking childhood vaccination practices to autism. Major medical and scientific reviews, including a 2025-2026 WHO evidence review, found no causal relationship between vaccines and autism.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420 on August 10, 2026, directing changes to federal childhood-vaccine recommendations and further review of the immunization schedule. The order called for spacing vaccinations across visits and recommended separate administration of measles, mumps, and rubella components once those products became available. During the signing event, Trump discussed autism and repeated claims linking childhood vaccination practices to autism. Those statements were remarks accompanying the order; they were not a finding in the order that vaccines cause autism. The World Health Organization’s September 2026 evidence review found no causal relationship between vaccines and autism spectrum disorder. The executive action concerns federal recommendations and agency review, while clinical guidance and individual vaccination decisions involve additional medical and public-health considerations. Distinguishing the text of the order from the president’s comments is important because the two carried different evidentiary weight. The signing established a federal policy process for revising recommendations, but did not convert the autism claim into a scientific conclusion. The event should be understood as an administrative change alongside public remarks that repeated a disputed claim.

title: Trump Was 'Very Surprised' Allies Wouldn't Join His Hormuz Adventure
description_short: Trump Was 'Very Surprised' Allies Wouldn't Join His Hormuz Adventure
description_medium: Trump said he was 'very surprised' Australia declined to send troops to the Strait of Hormuz, which is rich coming from a president who spent the week oscillating between begging allies for help and insisting he didn't need them. The significance is diplomatic and psychological at once: he keeps treating allied reluctance as betrayal rather than as a rational response to bad strategy. That is how coalition politics turns into a toddler grievance.
description_long: On March 21, 2026, Donald Trump said he was “very surprised” that Australia had declined to send troops to help secure the Strait of Hormuz. The comment came amid a fuel crisis and U.S. efforts to seek allied assistance in the region. The Guardian reported that Trump had asked Australia to contribute forces and reacted publicly when it refused. The episode showed a gap between the administration’s request for coalition support and the Australian government’s willingness to take part. It did not establish that Australia had previously committed troops or that refusal changed the military situation by itself. Other governments also weighed the risks of joining operations around the strait, a key route for global energy shipments. The exchange became a diplomatic disagreement over burden-sharing and the goals of the U.S. approach. Trump’s surprise comment is evidence of his response to the refusal, not proof that the alliance had broken down or that Australia endorsed Iran’s position. The broader dispute concerned whether partners would support U.S. policy and what role they would accept in a conflict that carried regional and economic risks.

title: Trump Taj Mahal Owed Contractors Tens of Millions After Opening
description_short: Trump Taj Mahal Owed Contractors Tens of Millions After Opening
description_medium: Fourteen weeks after the Trump Taj Mahal opened in Atlantic City, The Washington Post reported that unpaid bills were approaching $90 million. An attorney for a contractor said $72.8 million was owed to construction firms, and about 70 contractors were preparing to meet over whether to continue negotiations or sue. The record supports a substantial unpaid-contractor dispute at the Taj Mahal, but not the stored Trump Plaza/1992 framing or a blanket finding of fraud across Trump properties.
description_long: In July 1990, The Washington Post reported that unpaid construction bills at Donald Trump’s Taj Mahal casino in Atlantic City were approaching $90 million, roughly fourteen weeks after the property opened. An attorney for one contractor said construction firms were owed $72.8 million. About 70 contractors were preparing to meet to discuss whether to continue negotiations or file lawsuits. The report described a dispute over payment for work on the casino, with contractors facing uncertainty about whether they would recover the amounts claimed. It is a contemporaneous account of one property and one period. The facts do not establish a general practice across Trump’s businesses or a legal finding that the casino committed fraud. The distinction matters because later commentary sometimes treats the episode as proof of a broad pattern, while the cited reporting documents specific unpaid bills and planned legal action. The Taj Mahal opened in April 1990; the report appeared in July. It describes contractors’ claims and their options at that time, not the eventual outcome of every claim or any settlement reached later.

title: Mar-a-Lago Classified Documents Include Special Access Programs and Nuclear Info
description_short: Mar-a-Lago Classified Documents Include Special Access Programs and Nuclear Info
description_medium: When the FBI searched Mar-a-Lago in August 2022, agents recovered documents bearing highly sensitive classification markings, including Special Access Program labels. The search was part of an investigation into government records retained after Trump left office. Those markings indicated material subject to strict access controls, but do not by themselves show that a foreign party obtained the information. The search warrant and later filings described separate recovery totals.
description_long: The FBI executed a search warrant at Mar-a-Lago on August 8, 2022, as part of an investigation into government records retained after Donald Trump left office. The search recovered documents with classification markings, including material labeled for Special Access Programs, which impose additional controls on access and handling. The presence of those markings underscored the sensitivity of records kept at a private club. It did not establish that a foreign government had obtained them or that a specific intelligence loss occurred. The search was one stage in a broader records dispute: government documents had previously been returned in batches, and investigators sought additional records under a warrant. Totals reported at different points can refer to different collections, including records returned before the search and materials seized on August 8. They should not be merged as if all documents were found in the same location or during the same search. The documented issue was the custody and handling of sensitive government information after the end of Trump’s term. Claims about the precise exposure or damage require evidence beyond the classification markings themselves.

title: ICE Deportations to El Salvador's CECOT Mega-Prison
description_short: ICE Deportations to El Salvador's CECOT Mega-Prison
description_medium: In 2025, the Trump administration arranged to send some deportees to El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center, known as CECOT, under an agreement with President Nayib Bukele’s government. The United States paid El Salvador for detention. The transfers raised legal questions about notice, access to lawyers, and the opportunity to challenge removal before people entered foreign prison custody. Reports of harsh detention conditions also drew human-rights scrutiny.
description_long: In 2025, the Trump administration arranged for deported Venezuelan men to be held at El Salvador’s Terrorism Confinement Center, or CECOT, under an agreement with President Nayib Bukele’s government. The United States paid El Salvador for the detention arrangement. The transfers drew legal challenges because people sent abroad could face continued imprisonment while having limited access to lawyers and U.S. courts. Human-rights reporting described severe conditions at CECOT, including overcrowding and inadequate access to basic services. Those reports concern conditions at the prison and should be distinguished from proof about each individual detainee’s treatment. The central legal issue was whether the government could remove people to a foreign prison without meaningful notice and an opportunity to challenge the action. The arrangement also raised questions about U.S. responsibility when deportation results in detention by another government. The transfers were not a determination that every person sent to CECOT had committed a crime. Reporting on the policy documented both the government-to-government agreement and serious concerns about due process and confinement abroad. The specific circumstances and legal claims varied among detainees.

title: Trump: Proud Boys militia launches text campaign to recruit people for voter intimidation
description_short: Trump: Proud Boys militia launches text campaign to recruit people for voter intimidation
description_medium: Less than two days after Trump told the Proud Boys to “stand by” during the September 2020 presidential debate, the group launched an automated text-message campaign seeking recruits for Election Day activity described as voter intimidation. The campaign came to public attention through a social-media post. The available account does not establish its reach or that intimidation occurred, so the messages document an organizing effort rather than completed interference.
description_long: Less than two days after Donald Trump told the Proud Boys to “stand by” during the September 2020 presidential debate, the group launched an automated text-message campaign seeking recruits for Election Day activity described as voter intimidation. The campaign came to public attention through a social-media post. The messages sought people willing to participate in the group’s proposed election-related activity, but the reported account does not state how many people received them or whether anyone acted on the call. That distinction matters: an effort to recruit for intimidation is evidence of organizing, but it does not by itself prove that voters were actually threatened or prevented from voting. The timing drew attention because the campaign followed Trump’s nationally televised remarks to the group. The available facts do not establish that his debate comment directed the text campaign or that the group coordinated with his campaign. The episode therefore documents a sequence of public rhetoric and extremist-group recruitment while leaving the size and result of the effort unresolved. Any claim about actual voter intimidation or operational coordination would require evidence beyond the text campaign itself.

title: Trump: Nvidia buys favor with Trump by investing in Intel, FTC approves
description_short: Trump: Nvidia buys favor with Trump by investing in Intel, FTC approves
description_medium: The Federal Trade Commission approved Nvidia’s proposed $5 billion investment in Intel on December 19. The companies also announced plans to cooperate on data-center and personal-computer technology. The investment and approval are documented corporate and regulatory actions. The associated claim that Nvidia was buying political favor with Trump is an allegation about motive; the available account does not establish an exchange or connect the approval to presidential intervention.
description_long: The Federal Trade Commission approved Nvidia’s proposed $5 billion investment in Intel on December 19. The companies also said they planned to cooperate on technology for data centers and personal computers. The transaction brought together two major U.S. semiconductor firms at a time when domestic chip manufacturing and computing infrastructure were prominent policy issues. The reporting framed Nvidia’s investment as a way to gain favor with President Donald Trump, but the investment itself does not establish that motive. The available facts describe regulatory approval, the amount proposed, and the companies’ planned cooperation; they do not document an exchange of political benefits or a particular intervention by Trump. The companies also did not confirm whether the deal would result in additional U.S. manufacturing. Those distinctions separate what happened from claims about why it happened and what it might deliver. The approval allowed the investment to proceed, while the expected commercial effects and any effect on domestic production remained uncertain. The episode illustrates the political attention surrounding major technology investments, but does not establish improper influence or a quid pro quo.

title: Trump: Senate Republicans agree that Donald Trump won by colluding with Russia
description_short: Trump: Senate Republicans agree that Donald Trump won by colluding with Russia
description_medium: On August 18, 2020, the Republican-controlled Senate Intelligence Committee released the fifth volume of its investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. The report examined contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian-linked figures, including the campaign’s relationship with Paul Manafort and Konstantin Kilimnik. It documented extensive interactions and counterintelligence concerns, but did not conclude that the campaign criminally conspired with the Russian government.
description_long: On August 18, 2020, the Republican-controlled Senate Intelligence Committee released the fifth and final volume of its bipartisan investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. The report examined contacts between the Trump campaign and Russian-linked figures, including campaign chairman Paul Manafort and Konstantin Kilimnik, whom the committee identified as a Russian intelligence officer. It described extensive contacts and assessed that Manafort’s access to campaign information created a serious counterintelligence risk. The committee also found that Russia sought to influence the election and that the campaign welcomed assistance from Moscow. The report did not conclude that the Trump campaign criminally conspired with the Russian government. That distinction matters because the title’s shorthand can blur documented contacts and counterintelligence concerns with a finding of criminal collusion. The Senate investigation involved bipartisan staff work and a Republican-led committee, but its conclusions were not a criminal judgment. It supplied a detailed account of Russian activity and campaign contacts while drawing a narrower legal conclusion than the phrase “won through collusion” would suggest.

title: Donald Trump letter accuses street vendor veterans of destroying the city
description_short: Donald Trump letter accuses street vendor veterans of destroying the city
description_medium: In June 2004, Donald Trump wrote to New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg about street vendors working near Trump Tower. Trump described Fifth Avenue as “deplorable,” said the vendors were “rapidly destroying” the street, and questioned whether some were veterans. The letter sought city action concerning the vendors, but the available account does not establish what the city did or whether the military-service claims were accurate.
description_long: On or shortly before June 17, 2004, Donald Trump sent New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg a letter about street vendors near Trump Tower. Trump called conditions on Fifth Avenue “deplorable” and said the vendors were “rapidly destroying” the street. He also questioned whether some vendors who identified themselves as veterans had served in the military. The letter asked the mayor to address the vendors, placing a complaint about the area around Trump’s property before city government. The episode documents Trump’s own language and his request for municipal action. It does not establish how many vendors were affected, whether Bloomberg or city agencies changed enforcement, or whether the claims about veterans were verified. Those limits matter because the letter’s accusations were claims made by Trump, not findings by the city. The available account supports reporting the request and its terms, but not a broader conclusion about city policy or the vendors’ military histories. The letter shows one instance of Trump using a direct appeal to a mayor to press for regulation of street activity near his building.
